prompt: Can you explain what inflation actually is and why it's bad if wages go up too? I never really got it.
text:
## What inflation is

Inflation is a general rise in prices over time. When it happens, one dollar buys less than it used to. If a basket of groceries cost $100 last year and costs $105 now, that's 5% inflation.

## Why it can be bad even when wages go up

What matters is not your paycheck's size but what it can buy. Economists call this your **real wage**.

- If prices rise 5% and your pay rises 5%, you're back where you started. You feel no better off, even though the number got bigger.
- If prices rise 5% and your pay rises 3%, you're effectively poorer.
- If your pay rises 7%, you're ahead.

So higher wages don't automatically cancel out inflation. Several things get in the way:

1. **Wages often lag behind prices.** Raises usually come once a year, but prices can jump any week. In between, you lose ground.
2. **Not everyone's pay rises equally.** Some people get big raises, and others get none. Retirees on fixed incomes are hit hardest.
3. **Savings lose value.** If you hold $10,000 in cash and prices rise 5%, that money buys about 5% less. A raise doesn't fix that.
4. **Prices don't all rise at the same rate.** Rent, food, or gas may jump much more than average. If your pay rises with the average but your biggest bills rise faster, you still feel squeezed.
5. **It makes planning harder.** Businesses and families struggle to budget, sign contracts, or invest when they can't predict what things will cost.
6. **Wages and prices can chase each other.** If businesses raise prices to pay higher wages, and workers then ask for more raises, inflation can keep feeding itself.

## Is some inflation okay?

Yes. Most central banks aim for slow, steady inflation, around 2% a year. At that pace, wages can keep up easily, and it encourages spending and investing instead of hoarding cash. The trouble starts when inflation is fast or unpredictable.

**In short:** inflation is bad when prices rise faster than your income, or when it hits your savings and bills harder than it helps your pay.
